newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's Yates Security sees first year loss.
newsitem.headline: Australia's Yates Security sees first year loss.

text.p: Australian security alarm company Yates Security Ltd said it expected to make a A$371,000 net loss on sales of A$25.2 million in its first year of operation after a A$35 million capital raising.

The privately-owned Yates Security, which has recently been restructured from three separate companies, would not initially list on the Australian Stock Exchange, Yates chief executive and chairman Ian Yates told a briefing to launch the capital raising.

Yates said its offer of 140 million shares at 25 cents per share was aimed at small investors and Yates would not list on the stock exchange because of compliance costs and the need to maintain a stable register.
Yates' prospectus, which says the issue is a "speculative investment", forecasts profits rising to A$50.29 million by the end of the fifth year of operation on sales of A$236.9 million.

Within the first three years, prospectus figures show a loss per share of 0.1 cents per share in the first year, earnings per share of 0.7 cents per share in the second year and earnings per share of 5.2 cents per share.
That third year forecast translates into a issue price to earnings multiple of 4.8 times.

Accounts in the prospectus show the restructured group generated profits of A$19,420 on sales of A$1.05 million in the period from November 8 to December 31, 1997, while net cash held fell A$157,252 after negative cash flows from investing activities of A$477,125.
The prospectus did not include collated earnings data for the three companies for previous years.
Yates' total assets of A$49.01 million included A$40.44 million of goodwill.
Net of goodwill, there is an assets deficit of A$414,000.
Yates' family company will retain 160 million or 53 percent of the capital in the restructured group.
Yates said the offer was not currently being promoted by any broker, but he had had enquiries from some interested in promoting the issue.
In the meantime, Yates itself was promoting the issue directly to small investors.
The funds raised would largely be used to buy monitored phone lines.
Yates said he envisaged creating a group capable of monitoring home and other alarm systems through telephone lines using a network of franchisees offering security and communications products.
He said it would eventually be a global group.
